items.body: An Ada County judge will privately review data spreadsheets compiled by Boise State University researchers before ruling on whether the university must hand them over to an anti-abortion lobbying group. The Idaho Family Policy Center (IFPC) — a Christian lobbying group that helped write Idaho’s restrictive abortion laws — sued Boise State , alleging that it withheld public records related to a widely cited article co-authored by two researchers affiliated with the university. The article said that obstetrician-gynecologists fled Idaho after the state’s abortion ban took effect in 2022. Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin " data-large-file="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" class="size-full wp-image-127657" src="https://www.idahoednews.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/images.jpeg" alt="" width="150" height="200" /> Ada County District Court Judge Nancy Baskin In December, IFPC filed a records request seeking “all documents” and “all data” related to the article, but Boise State only provided a single, two-page spreadsheet. In a July petition to Ada County’s district court, IFPC argued that the research “must have produced a paper trail longer than two pages.” IFPC’s petition asked the court to compel the university to hand over additional records, including emails along with documents from Boise State’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), which approved the researchers’ process for collecting data on human subjects. District Judge Nancy Baskin heard arguments in the case Friday. Carsten Peterson, an attorney at Hawley Troxell, represented Boise State. While Peterson acknowledged that additional records related to the article exist, including various other data sets, he argued that the university reviewed IFPC’s request “in good faith” and provided the only record that matched its request. After asking the attorneys questions for more than an hour, Baskin ordered Boise State to show her any data files that the university deemed outside the scope of IFPC’s request. Baskin will review the spreadsheets “in-camera,” meaning behind closed doors, before she issues a written ruling on IFPC’s petition. Boise State has 10 days to deliver the spreadsheets to Baskin. items.body: The Idaho State Capitol building as seen on Jan. 23, 2024, in Boise. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho lawmakers will weigh whether to fund several drug-prevention and treatment projects, totaling over $3 million, through the state’s endowment fund from tobacco lawsuit settlement money. The legislative Joint Millennium Fund Committee, which oversees the endowment, heard 10 proposals Friday for use of the settlement money, which must go toward drug and alcohol prevention. As of Sept. 30, the fund’s balance was nearly $43.5 million — however, some of the previously approved projects hadn’t yet been funded, according to Senior Budget and Policy Analyst Janica Bisharat. The committee is focused particularly on youth prevention and cessation in approving use of the fund for projects. Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, (right) chats with Sen. Jim Woodward, R-Sagle, on the Senate floor on March 10, 2025, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) “I am laser-focused on prevention,” committee co-Chair Sen. Van Burtenshaw, R-Terreton, said Friday. “I have three deaths in my family already, and two or three more that are getting close. I’ve seen abuse. I’ve seen the problem, and as long as I have this position, I’m gonna focus on that. And that’s the focus of our group here is prevention.” The committee did not decide on its recommended projects to fund. The funding would need final approval from legislative budget writers on the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee during the legislative session, which begins in January. Here are the proposed projects lawmakers heard Friday: Recovery Idaho asks for $32,780 to create a certification process for recovery centers The nonprofit Recovery Idaho sought just under $33,000 to create a voluntary accreditation program for recovery centers statewide. Recovery centers provide treatment for drug and alcohol addiction and also often provide additional support for clients in treatment. “The problem right now is that the recovery community centers throughout the state are very well intentioned, but there’s a fair amount of variation and maybe not enough tracking of what exactly happens and what those outcomes are,” Andra Smith Hansen, a Recovery Idaho board member, told the committee members. Recovery centers provide support to adults, but many of those adults are parents, Smith Hansen said, and better outcomes for those adults can lead to better outcomes for their children. The money would be used to work with recovery centers statewide to develop standards, a process for accreditation and standardized metrics to evaluate outcomes. Foundation for the Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency seeks $28K to help train workforce The Idaho Conference on Alcohol and Drug Dependency has held a yearly conference for more than 40 years for behavioral healthcare workers, but participation is lagging and workers statewide aren’t always able to travel to the Treasure Valley for the conference, according to Leah Kalk, a board member of the foundation. Rep. Marco Erickson, R-Idaho Falls, makes a phone call from the House floor on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The foundation is seeking $28,000 for scholarships for healthcare workers statewide to travel to the conference and earn required continuing education credits. Rep. Trustees discussed a possible change to how the
items.body: The Pocatello-Chubbuck School District will stick with a five-day school week and trimester schedule after trustees unanimously rejected proposals to adopt a four-day week and semesters. The vote happened at a board meeting Tuesday and follows months of consideration that fleshed out trustees’ preferences for keeping the district’s schedules intact . Trustees discussed a possible change to how the district uses Fridays, but the board took no action. Two trustees proposed exploring different hybrid models, but neither motion received a second. “We have a consensus that we certainly do want to look at the options,” said Board Chair Raymond Knoff. “It probably is too late for us to do that this year.” The change to a four-day week would have made Pocatello-Chubbuck one of the largest districts in Idaho to adopt the model. The similarly sized Nampa district made the switch two years ago. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees each had their own concerns with the change. Trustee Megan Furniss cited concerns about a lack of input from the district’s families who qualify for free- and reduced-price lunch. Trustee Bill Osborn simply wanted to stay in line with most school districts in the country. “If it was such a good idea, why haven’t more school districts in the past five decades gone after it?” asked Osborn, echoing his statements at a recent meeting. Finances weren’t part of the five-day week or hybrid discussions. “In my opinion, it shouldn’t be part of the conversation,” said district business manager Jonathan Balls, “just because there’s a lot bigger factors out there than the finances.”

items.body: October is Dyslexia Awareness Month in Idaho, and over the past 10 years, Idaho professionals have prioritized early literacy and dyslexia education statewide. From updated, data-driven instruction for incoming teachers to intervention tutoring for elementary students, Boise State University has been at the forefront of these literacy initiatives. In September, Boise State University awarded its first endowed professorship in education to Clinical Associate Professor Carolyn Cort. Her specialty is early literacy. At BSU, Cort teaches courses in the early language and literacy endorsement, which is similar to a minor, for education majors and teacher candidates. The classes instruct teacher candidates how to properly test literacy comprehension and screen for dyslexia. Panelists at Saturday’s Literacy, Language and Dyslexia Summit at BSU. items.body: Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron presents on the agency’s budget to the Legislature’s Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee on Jan. 27, 2026. (Kyle Pfannenstiel/Idaho Capital Sun) The director of Idaho’s largest state agency will step down by the end of the year. Idaho Department of Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron told employees in a letter she’d be stepping back to provide more support to her family, Boise State Public Radio first reported. Gov. Brad Little’s communication director, Emily Callihan, told BSPR that Charron’s father faced “significant health challenges.” “This has not been an easy decision,” Charron wrote in the letter to employees. “The past year has brought significant challenges for my family, and I realize that they need more of my time, attention, and support. Family has always been important to me, and right now, being there for mine needs to be my priority.” Charron’s last day has not been finalized, and it’s unclear who will serve as interim director when she leaves. Idaho Gov. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Little appointed Charron as director in July 2025, and she officially stepped into the post in September last year, after previously serving as the agency’s top Medicaid official since 2021, the Idaho Capital Sun reported. “I want to thank Juliet Charron for her outstanding service as Health and Welfare Director,” Little said in a written statement to the Sun. “Under her leadership, the department made meaningful progress in strengthening child welfare prevention, preparing to distribute nearly $200 million in Rural Health Transformation funding in the coming months as part of nearly $1 billion over five years, and improving compliance, accountability, and program outcomes. I appreciate her commitment to serving Idahoans and look forward to announcing new leadership for the state’s largest agency before the end of the year.” Health and Welfare spokesman AJ McWhorter told the Sun the agency had “a number of vacancies in some key positions for a variety of unrelated reasons, including external opportunities, retirements, and personal and family reasons.” “The Governor’s Office will announce a new director at a later date,” McWhorter said. “DHW is hiring for the other positions, and we encourage qualified people to apply. We will continue to focus on the work and provide quality, efficient, and effective services for the people of Idaho.” Before joining Idaho’s health agency, Charron held leadership positions in the Texas Medicaid program and with the Texas Office of Inspector General. She also worked in government programs and “compliance roles” for a community-based health plan in Arizona, according to her biography . Charron leaves Idaho’s largest agency with the biggest budget The Idaho Department of Health and Welfare runs public assistance programs like Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and the Women and Infant Children program. The health department also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, provides child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds. As head of the agency, Charron oversaw some of the beginning stages of the state’s shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies , as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345 . The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030. Charron has also overseen the influx of federal funds from the Rural Health Transformation Grant. items.body: How much growth is too much, and too fast? The State Board of Education grappled with that question last week, and couldn’t wrestle it into submission. The board punted on a three-year plan that guides new growth and new programs at the state’s colleges and universities. In its stead, the board gave the schools a one-year go-ahead, enough to let them keep working on new programs for 2027-28. The three-year plan is on hold until the board’s December meeting. Yes, three-year plans are wonky and boring. Until you think about what’s being planned. If you’re a taxpayer, here’s why you ought to care. The whole idea behind the three-year plan is to grow the higher education portfolio in an orderly way — without wasting tax dollars on redundant programs. If you’re student, or soon to be one, here’s why you ought to care. These plans will help determine what you can study, and where, laying out your options for career credentials or a full-blown degree. And if you’re an employer, here’s why you ought to care. Many of the new additions to the three-year plans focus on the state’s hottest job sectors — such as healthcare and cybersecurity. These are the new programs Idaho employers need: pipelines from the campus to the workplace. So the State Board is debating something that sounds dull, but is actually crucial. Who wants what? Here’s what Idaho’s eight colleges and universities hope to add by 2030, according to three-year plans submitted to the State Board of Education. The eight colleges and universities are looking at creating 277 new programs over the next three years. Nearly half of these new adds, 111 in all, are professional certificates, and 61 are career-technical programs. The remaining 105 are undergraduate or graduate degree programs. items.body: From left to right: Coeur d'Alene attorney Arthur "Art" Macomber, former Idaho Congressman Raúl Labrador and incumbent Idaho Attorney General Lawrence Wasden debate on Idaho Public Television on April 19, 2022. (Photo by Aaron Kunz/Idaho Public Television) During the 2026 election cycle, Idaho voters have had very few opportunities to see Republican incumbents answer questions at live, public events. For years it was the norm for major candidates in statewide and federal races to appear live and debate each other. Journalist Betsy Z. Russell asks a candidate question during an Idaho Public Television debate on May 6, 2016. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger) “It was a tradition in Idaho,” said Betsy Russell, former longtime president of the Idaho Press Club and current president for Idahoans for Openness in Government. “That was how candidates, including incumbents seeking reelection, got out there and put their views and how they contrasted with those of their opponents, in front of all voters all across the state of Idaho.” Idaho Public Television, which for years has broadcast its Idaho Debates series statewide, did not have the staffing to put on the events this year, according to Melissa Davlin, IPTV producer and Idaho Press Club president. “I do think there are some incumbents who would have said yes to debates had that been a possibility,” Davlin said. Davlin also noted that there’s a national trend of candidates from both major parties declining debates. Of the 35 U.S. Senate seats up for election this year, 21 of them had no debate between the major candidates, ABC News reported. Similarly, of the 36 governors up for election, 21 of those races had no debate scheduled between two major-party candidates. “This is not Idaho-specific,” Davlin said. “… and you could say a big part of that is the siloing of social media. People who are running for office often have or feel like they have a direct line to voters.” The League of Women Voters of Idaho this year held forums for U.S. Senate candidates and gubernatorial candidates . The Republican incumbents in both of those races declined to participate. U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s campaign spokesman previously told the Sun that he declined that forum because the individual who reached out to him to ask about participation had endorsed his opponent. The league’s president Jean Henscheid told the Sun that individual, former state Rep. Julie Yamamoto, had reached out in her own capacity and was not one of the event’s organizers. The head of the state’s Department of Health and Welfare will step down by the end of 2026. Juliet Charron is resigning after 13 months on the job. The policies are all identical, word-for-word, except for the districts’ names. “This Policy is only to aid Homedale School Distri
items.body: Trained teachers and staff will carry guns in Marsing and Homedale schools after trustees in both districts unanimously approved policies last week. The armed staff policies are modeled after one in the Kimberly School District , which rolled out its program last year. The policies are all identical, word-for-word, except for the districts’ names. “This Policy is only to aid Homedale School District in deterring, detecting, and denying some type of active shooter incident from occurring on school property,” Homedale’s policy reads. Approved staff members carrying a firearm will “be responsible to defend, using deadly force, if necessary, their zone of responsibility.” The Homedale and Marsing school boards must now approve individual staff members to carry a concealed firearm on campus. Criteria for approval include: Possession of a current Idaho Enhanced Concealed Weapon License A recommendation from the superintendent A physical and psychological assessment The board can deny permission for any reason and will review staff members’ grants of permission annually. Once approved, employees must complete at least 40 hours of training. “Training will include engagement on the range with a certified instructor in live fire situations that require ‘shoot, don’t shoot’ decision making and other dynamic scenarios,” the policy says. District leaders said they heard mostly positive feedback from community members. “Every community member that I’ve talked to … has been super positive, saying we should’ve done this years ago,” Marsing Board Chair Jason Sevy told Idaho Education News. On Monday, after approving the policy, Homedale held a community meeting to gather feedback. Dwayne Fisher told EdNews he only heard positive feedback. Trustees in both districts had been considering the policy for years. Marsing surveyed its employees in 2022 but didn’t act until this year. Days after both districts approved their policies, a school shooter killed four people at Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon. Megan Lambert , a Boise State University graduate and special education teacher, died in the shooting. “W ith what just happened in Bend, u nfortunately, it’s on the forefront of everyone’s minds again,” Fisher said. “More than anything, we’re hoping that people know our schools are not going to be soft targets.” Both districts have begun installing signs showing that staff members may be armed.

items.body: Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios, but high costs to build such projects can create barriers. (Photo by Gregory Thomas/USDA) High costs and lengthy permitting processes are two of the barriers to bringing nuclear-powered electricity to customers in Idaho, officials from three electrical utilities told state regulators during a public forum outside of Boise on Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Officials from Idaho Power, Rocky Mountain Power and Avista told members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission that nuclear energy can provide a reliable and clean source of energy that diversifies energy portfolios. However, the high cost to build nuclear power projects, the absence of price certainty and permitting processes that can stretch for 10 years or longer do not align with state regulators’ “least cost, least risk” mandate. “When I think of the benefits of nuclear, I think diversity is a huge part of it,” Idaho Power Chief Operating Officer Adam Richins said. “Obviously, it’s dispatchable clean energy, which really doesn’t exist besides nuclear.” Adam Richins was named Idaho Power’s executive vice president and chief operating officer in February 2026 after previously serving in other roles at the utility. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Power) “On the other side of the spectrum … right now we don’t know how much it’s going to cost, and obviously when you talk about ‘least cost, least risk,’ that is very important,” Richins said. For example, Richins said the expansion of Plant Vogtle nuclear power plant in Georgia ran over budget by $16 billion to $21 billion. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission sets rates and regulates investor-owned and privately-owned utilities that provide electricity, gas, water or some telephone services for a profit. The three members of the Idaho Public Utilities Commission, or PUC for short, are appointed by the governor. None of the three companies use nuclear in their energy mix. But Rocky Mountain Power officials recently announced a 40-year power purchase agreement to buy electricity from a TerraPower nuclear power plant that is being built in Kemmerer, Wyoming. The Wyoming plant is being built at the site of a coal plant that is being retired, with about $2 billion in federal funding from the U.S. Department of Energy supporting the project. The Idaho Public Utilities Commission did not have any specific nuclear energy proposals under consideration during Tuesday’s forum and did not take any action. “The primary purpose of this opportunity for us is to listen to each and every one (of the utilities participating in the forum),” Idaho PUC Chairman Edward Lodge said. items.body: A 46-year-old graduate student, a 12-year-old homeschooler and an 18-year-old college freshman gathered with others on a sunny Tuesday afternoon at Moscow High to kick off the last week of an archeological dig. The dig is part of a continuing push by the university’s anthropology department to help Idahoans connect to their own history through archeology — and connect with each other through a shared interest. This fall marks the third time the group has dug at the high school, built in the 1930s. Organizers say it was also the most productive, with students discovering a corner of the original 1890 school that was demolished years ago to make way for the current high school. Students also dug in what was once an alley behind area homes, uncovering artifacts of daily life, like buttons, a doll face and remnants of dishes. Graduate students recently started a project underneath Moscow’s public library, where they discovered hundreds of intact literary artifacts, like bookbinding supplies, ink pads and lightbulbs. The program provides students with real-world experience that is typically offered through a field school, where they often pay to travel to a remote location to complete a dig during a school break. Other community members are also welcome to participate. “It gives them more than just the skills training — it gives them the why,” said Katrina Eichner, associate professor of anthropology. “It’s not just fun for us to play in the dirt. This is important to people because it’s their history.” University of Idaho anthropology professors Katrina Eichner and Renae Campbell help students at an archaeological dig at Moscow High. Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane , who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation. McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands. The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690. In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. Educational exhibits are placed along the trail to provide information. (Photo courtesy of the National Park Service) The Friends of Minidoka nonprofit will host its 2026 symposium, which will feature a film screening, legal discussion and lecture, “to consider the enduring importance of due process, equal protection, and civic engagement in protecting our civil liberties and strengthening democracy,” according to a press release from the organization. The 2026 Civil Liberties Symposium, titled Law, Civil Liberties, and the Continuing Pursuit of Justice: From Wayne Collins to Today, will examine how “the unjust incarceration of Japanese Americans during World War II continues to inform contemporary debates surrounding immigration, detention, national security, and constitutional rights,” the press release said. In 1942, the Minidoka War Relocation Center was constructed in Jerome County at Hunt, Idaho. Locally, it was known as “Hunt Camp.” While in operation, the site was the seventh largest city in Idaho, incarcerating nearly 9,400 people at its peak population. (Photo courtesy of the National Archives and Records Administration) The series begins Thursday with a screening of “Wayne Collins: One Fighting Irishman,” a 30-minute documentary about the San Francisco attorney who spent more than two decades defending Japanese Americans who renounced their U.S. citizenship under duress while imprisoned at the Tule Lake Segregation Center during World War II. The screening will be followed by a discussion with Emily Croston, staff attorney with the ACLU of Idaho, and Wendy Olson, former U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho and chairwoman of the Idaho State Bar’s Diversity Section. On Nov. 5, the group will host its 2026 distinguished lecture: “Mass Deportation, Detention, and ICE: How We Got Here and What We Can Do,” presented by Kari Hong, the director of the Immigration Law Clinic at the University of Idaho College of Law. Drawing on her experience as an immigration attorney, public interest lawyer, and legal scholar, Hong will examine the history and present-day realities of immigration enforcement and detention, along with opportunities to protect the rights of affected individuals. The lecture will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the audience. The symposium concludes Dec. 8 with an online presentation of Hong’s distinguished lecture, offering another opportunity for community members to participate and engage with these issues. “History reminds us that civil liberties can be threatened when fear and claims of national security are used to justify the erosion of constitutional protections,” said Robyn Achilles, executive director of Friends of Minidoka. “By bringing historical perspectives into conversation with today’s legal challenges, the Civil Liberties Symposium creates opportunities for our community to learn, ask difficult questions, and consider our shared responsibility to uphold justice.” All events are free and open to the public, with registration required. items.body: An orange "detour ahead" sign alerts motorists of a new route around new housing construction in Boise in summer 2026. (Photo by Abigail Gerstein/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s newly approved Opportunity Zones could help bring more housing, businesses and jobs to communities across the state. The attraction for investors is the potential tax savings. This month, Idaho Commerce announced that the U.S. Treasury approved 25 zones, including areas in Boise, Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls. The new Opportunity Zone designations take effect Jan. 1. An Opportunity Zone is a designated area where the federal government offers tax benefits to encourage private investment. The idea is straightforward: give investors a financial reason to put money into communities that could benefit from more economic activity. In Boise, the five areas identified by the city are Downtown, Shoreline, University District, South Boise Village and West Boise . These are general descriptions of the selected areas. The actual boundaries determine whether a particular property is included. In North Idaho, the officially designated list includes parts of Coeur d’Alene and Post Falls, as well as areas around Blanchard and Kellogg, Smelterville and Wardner. Other designated communities include Caldwell, Garden City, Nampa, Pocatello and Twin Falls. The state’s announcement provides the complete list and a link to look up the boundaries . The program connects investors with projects that need money. An investor who sells stock, real estate or a business at a profit may face a tax bill on that gain. By investing an eligible gain through a special investment vehicle called a Qualified Opportunity Fund, the investor may receive tax benefits. The fund puts that money into qualifying property or businesses within a zone. The IRS explains the basic structure here . Imagine a business owner who sells a company and wants to invest some of the profit. Across town, a developer wants to turn an underused property into apartments with shops on the ground floor. If the project is in an Opportunity Zone and meets the program’s requirements, an Opportunity Fund could connect that investor’s money with the development. The investor receives an ownership interest, and the project receives money to help move forward. Under the new rules beginning in 2027, a qualifying investor generally can delay tax on the invested gain for five years and reduce the amount of that gain subject to tax. Holding the investment for at least 10 years may also allow the investor to avoid federal tax on qualifying growth in the investment’s value. Coeur d’Alene also offers a potential partnership story. Idaho Capital Sun reported that Kootenai County and the Coeur d’Alene Tribe both sought designation for the local tract. The application summary identified vacant tribal land as an opportunity for investment involving the Tribe, local governments, and private developers. That possibility deserves attention, although the designation itself does not establish a finalized development partnership. For investors, those benefits can make a long-term investment more attractive. For developers and business owners, the program can help attract money from people willing to wait for a project to mature. That could support a new apartment building, the redevelopment of an older commercial property, or the expansion of a qualifying business. Residents may benefit from additional homes, employment, and services. Those outcomes are possibilities, not promises. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

items.body: Work continues on the new QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. Today’s data center buildout has become the largest industrial boom since the railroad era of the 19th century, with $10 trillion in investment and almost twice the economic impact. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch) The sheer size of investment in data centers is drawing concern as it surpasses all other historical booms and crowds out other more job-creating ventures. Until now, no industry had driven the U.S. economy with such force since the railroad expansion of the late 1800s, when titans battled one another to lay the transcontinental tracks that would connect America from coast to coast. Railroads in the 19 th century consumed about $173 billion in today’s dollars and created more than 2% of the nation’s annual economic output (GDP) over 20 years. Today’s data center buildout will dwarf that amount, with $10 trillion in investment, and now have almost twice the economic impact — nearly 4% of GDP. That’s according to a report created by a Columbia Business School professor, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. States are starting to feel left out of the windfall, many having granted tax exemptions before the boom. Years ago, before artificial intelligence prompted a tsunami of building, states typically welcomed data centers supporting internet traffic, offering tax abatements and other perks. Many officials now are rethinking that approach as tax revenues take a bigger hit and high energy demands take a toll on affordability. Nevada , for instance, trimmed tax abatements and will ask data centers to agree to foot the bill for energy and water demands, in a September executive order from Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo. States where data center costs will be concentrated over the three years are Texas ($638 billion), Virginia ($249 billion), Ohio ($169 billion) and Georgia ($160 billion), according to projections from Industrial Info Resources, a market intelligence firm. Southern states dominate the landscape for the number of data centers planned, with large numbers also proposed in Arizona, California, Florida, Indiana, Iowa, Indiana, North Carolina, Oregon, Pennsylvania and Washington state, according to a Pew Research Center report in April. The profitability of AI has yet to catch up with the expense of the buildout. “It is not a pretty picture right now,” said IIR’s senior vice president of research, David Pickering. “I think it will become profitable once things settle down a bit and more legislation is put in place to regulate how we handle AI. “The big players will no doubt find a way to make it profitable,” he said. There are signs the staggering cost of data centers is crowding out other investments such as housing. Over the past two years new construction value for data centers has more than doubled to $85 billion annually, while all other construction value has dropped 8%, according to a Stateline analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data as of August. As new data center value grew by $48 billion since 2024, new houses and apartments dropped by $29 billion, according to the data. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue, but for many others it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. (Photo courtesy of Alliance for Youth Action) Editor’s Note: This story is part of Gen Z at the Ballot Box, a collaboration between States Newsroom and The 19th . Boise State University senior Cade Syvock opposes abortion. As president of the school’s chapter of the conservative group Turning Point USA, the organization founded by the late activist Charlie Kirk, Syvock helped coordinate anti-abortion protests on campus. But he’s not spending much time this fall campaigning against an Idaho ballot initiative that would restore abortion access. Not for lack of interest — he calls the proposed law “very, very extreme” because it allows abortions after viability in certain emergency cases — but because of pressing economic issues he’d rather be working on. “It’s not like everybody’s going out and getting abortions 24/7, but everybody is trying to find a home,” Syvock said. In Idaho and Missouri, where voters will decide the future of abortion access on Nov. 3, campaigns are trying to reach a generation dealing with rising living costs and skepticism toward politics. For some young voters, abortion remains a defining issue. But for many others, it ranks behind more immediate economic concerns. Idaho’s initiative would restore abortion access. Missouri’s measure seeks to reinstate a near-total ban jettisoned by voters two years ago. People pushing for and against both measures are making their appeals to young voters, using social media and canvassing to increase turnout on Election Day, but they’re competing against other issues for Generation Z’s attention. “I’m not saying that the abortion stuff is any less important than housing, but I think in terms of what young people are focusing on right now, it’s definitely dropped a little bit,” Syvock said. Gen Z politicians who want to make a change grapple with parties that aren’t always ready for them In most elections, it’s difficult for campaigns to achieve high turnout among young voters, especially in between presidential election cycles. Less than half of the 40 million Gen Z Americans between ages 18 and 29 who were eligible to vote in 2024 cast a ballot, a study by the Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement at Tufts University found. This year, the number of eligible Gen Z-age voters is estimated at nearly 50 million. But there are some signs that turnout could be higher this year. Nonpartisan youth vote organization The Civics Center noted a significant increase in voter registration among 18-year-olds compared with the 2022 midterms, from 35% to 42%. And the Tufts survey points out that there are many signs Gen Z is active and engaged on political subjects, but that connecting issues to candidates and ballot questions is the challenge. The majority of Gen Z adults support abortion access, according to a September poll from The 19th and YouGov. But there’s a gender gap: Women were more likely than men to say abortion should be always or mostly legal, 69% to 51%. Almost half of men versus 31% of women say it should be mostly or always illegal. The number of Generation Z Missourians who got involved in the 2024 initiative petition is not available, but more than 110,000 Idahoans signed the petition to put abortion access on the state ballot. About 7% of those signatures came from people between the ages of 18 and 25, and twice as many of those signatures came from women than from men. But some organizing efforts are made more difficult by local politics as well as increasing costs for food, housing and transportation. The 19th/YouGov poll found that 21% of Gen Z adults were worried about their ability to pay for groceries and 34% were somewhat worried. But Raúl Labrador , the Republican incumbent running for a second term, says he transformed the office for the better — pointing to his legal victories defending state laws in court — in part because he followed through on a promise he made when he first campaigned: being an aggressive attorney general. The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election. The attorney general is an elected office that serves as the state’s top attorney, which includes defending the state and its laws in court, and serves on the Idaho Land Board, which manages state endowment lands. The attorney general serves a four-year term and receives an annual salary of $146,730. In a Republican-controlled state, Hickman’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic attorney general more than 30 years ago. She hasn’t run for public office before. She spent her childhood moving around the country as part of a military family. She said she has lived for 30 years in Idaho, where she said her family has deep roots. In 2013, she joined the Boise-based law firm McFarland Ritter as an attorney focusing on business negotiation and litigation. She served as board chair for Mormon Women for Ethical Government, a nonpartisan and 501(c)(4) faith-based nonprofit organization that joined a lawsuit unsuccessfully challenging an Idaho law that established tax credits for students to attend private, religious schools. items.body: Teachers in Bonneville School District will soon be required to sign a form certifying that they are either a biological male or female. District leaders say the new requirement will ensure compliance with state law governing public school bathroom usage. Multi-occupancy school restrooms must be designated for either males or females and only members of those biological sexes are allowed to enter, as required under Senate Bill 1100 , passed in 2023. “As a public school district, we have a responsibility to comply with Idaho law, regardless of our individual perspectives about it,” Superintendent Scott Woolstenhulme wrote in a letter to employees on Thursday. Woolstenhulme asked the school board to establish a “consistent process for employee verification.” Trustees on Wednesday night approved a resolution directing the superintendent to create a form that district employees must sign certifying their biological sex, as defined in Idaho code : “Male” means an individual who has, had, will have, or but for developmental or genetic anomaly or historical accident, would have the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports, and utilizes sperm for fertilization. “Female” means an individual who has, had, or will have, or but for developmental or genetic anomaly or historical accident, would have the reproductive system that at some point produces, transports, and utilizes eggs for fertilization. Idaho law — as established through 2024’s House Bill 421 — also declares that in human beings there are only two sexes, male and female. It was sponsored by Rep. Julianne Young, R-Blackfoot, and Rep. Bruce Skaug, R-Nampa. “An individual’s sex can be observed or clinically verified at or before birth; Rare disorders of sexual development are not exceptions to the binary nature of sex; In no case is an individual’s sex determined by stipulation or self identification,” Idaho law states. items.body: (UPDATED, 4:12 p.m. Tuesday, with comments from Secretary of State Phil McGrane.) In other states, even conservative strongholds like Kansas , voters have upheld abortion rights. But the abortion debate is not in Kansas anymore. Now it’s in Idaho. And it’s open warfare. Supporters and opponents have raised $9.7 million — so far — in the campaign over Proposition 1, a voter initiative to rescind Idaho’s near-complete abortion ban. Proposition 1 is by far the biggest political battle in the state, and, sensing opportunity, everyone wants a piece of the action. “Both sides are working to mobilize people to vote on that issue,” said Jaclyn Kettler, a political science professor at Boise State University. Proposition 1, explained For a quick and useful overview of what Proposition 1 would do, here’s a summary from Idaho Capital Sun . That also makes Proposition 1 a wild card. The hottest item on the ballot could drive turnout in other Nov. 3 elections — such as the governor’s and the state superintendent’s races; legislative races in Idaho’s scattered swing districts; and the $307 million in school levy requests . The high-powered opposition But for now, let’s focus on Proposition 1 itself. The parochial and partisan opposition is impossible to ignore. The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has contributed $1 million in opposition to Proposition 1 . The Catholic Diocese of Boise has contributed $300,000 . The Idaho Republican Party, meanwhile, has gone all-in against Proposition 1. State GOP chairwoman Dorothy Moon has made the initiative nearly a staple of the weekly op-ed she sends to news outlets; six of her last 10 op-eds mentioned Proposition 1 in whole or in part. Last week, the GOP rolled out a news release touting near unanimous opposition to Proposition 1, from statewide elected officials and Idaho’s congressional delegation. “If there is one issue that unites Republicans across the ideological spectrum, it is that of life,” Moon said. (The only name not on the list: Secretary of State Phil McGrane. Asked about it Tuesday, Moon deferred to McGrane. On Thursday afternoon, McGrane described himself as a pro-life Catholic and a pro-life Republican, but said, as the state’s elections official he is staying neutral on Proposition 1. “It’s important that everyone has confidence in the process,” McGrane told EdNews.) For many Republicans, the Proposition 1 fight is more than just a little personal. After all, the initiative challenges abortion restrictions passed by an overwhelmingly Republican Legislature — and signed into law by Gov. Brad Little, who is seeking a third term next month. Little last week voiced his opposition to Proposition 1, saying it would “make abortion far more accessible in Idaho.” For the state’s prevailing party — and for two of the state’s largest religious groups — fighting Proposition 1 is a matter of seeking to protect the status quo. Olivia Luna, a 21-year-old Idaho college student and Babe Vote leader, said a pair of 2023 state laws that removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting hurt students and young people especially hard. House Bill 124 removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification for voting. House Bill 340 also removed student IDs as an acceptable form of identification and standardized voter registration requirements for in-person registration and online registration. House Bill 340 also required the Idaho Transportation Department to create and offer no-fee identification cards that are accepted for voting. Luna said many students frequently move between their parents’ house, dorms and apartments throughout their academic career, making it difficult to prove residency from a list of documents accepted by the state. (Photo courtesy of Babe Vote) For people who don’t drive and don’t have a driver’s license, or for students who have a current out-of-state driver’s license, Luna said state voting requirements create unnecessary hurdles for young people to exercise their constitutional right to vote. “I would say it puts up a pretty significant road block for most students,” Luna said. Luna said Babe Vote paused its voter registration efforts after the laws took effect, and the laws continue to make Babe Vote’s voter registration and outreach efforts difficult. Luna said she appreciates the opportunities to work with McGrane’s office. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE In September 2023, state officials used water sampling to c onfirm the presence of quagga mussel larvae for the first time in state history. During water sampling this year, state officials found eight veliger mussels, the larvae form of the mussels, Tewalt said during a meeting of the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Committee at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Scuba divers also found what Tewalt described as “a number of adult mussels” while searching the Snake River. The mussels, which were discovered in the Snake River near Twin Falls, can reproduce extremely rapidly, clog pipes and cover boat hulls. If left unchecked, Tewalt said the spread of quagga mussels poses serious threats to the state’s drinking and irrigation water, recreation industry, state budget and economy. Need to get in touch? Have a news tip? CONTACT US In an effort to completely eradicate all of the invasive species, officials with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture have been administering lethal copper chemicals into the affected part of the Snake River each year since the mussels were first detected. Compared to previous years, the amount of mussels discovered in water sampling is lower and the affected section of the Snake River is smaller this year, Tewalt told legislators. “What it would signify is a very small population,” Tewalt said. After detecting the mussels again this summer, the ag department moved forward with another round of copper-based treatments – with scuba divers injecting the chemicals in harder to reach nooks, crannies and fissures in rock. Chanel Tewalt serves as the director of the Idaho Department of Agriculture. (Courtesy of Idaho State Department of Agriculture) “Copper in the water means that reproduction cycle (for the mussels) is halted,” Tewalt said. Along with mussels, the copper also kills fish and other aquatic life in the river. This year, Tewalt said there have been fewer fish killed and that state officials are not stocking the sections of the river being treated with copper with new fish. Although the mussels were first discovered in water samples in 2023, Tewalt told legislators the mussels have likely been in the Twin Falls pool of the Snake River for longer. Water sampling and monitoring for quagga mussels is an ongoing, years-long process. When water temperatures warm up again next year, state officials will resume water sampling to check for more quagga mussels, state officials said. YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. SUPPORT

items.body: Boise State University athletics has the green light to go $18 million in the red. With some reluctance, the State Board of Education approved the deficit spending plan Wednesday afternoon. Most of the $18 million will go into “revenue sharing” — direct payments to student-athletes. And Boise State will use a variety of budget reserves to cover the $18 million. “I personally don’t even like the term … deficit in athletics,” Boise State President David Hahn told State Board members. “Boise State is not running a deficit. We are managing our reserves, we are managing our finances. I’m putting that capital where it needs to be for success of all of the missions.” The $18 million figure is not necessarily unexpected. In August, Boise State Athletic Director Jeramiah Dickey warned the State Board that the cost of revenue sharing — and expenses tied to a move from the Mountain West Conference to a reformed Pac-12 conference — would drive the program into the red. Wednesday’s meeting brought the budget picture into more focus. Boise State is now projecting a $16.9 million deficit for the current budget year, which ends June 30. In August, Dickey pegged this year’s deficit at $14 million to $18 million. The university will provide the athletic department $3 million for debt service. The athletic department hopes to clear $2 million from special events at Albertsons Stadium. The stadium hosted two nights of the Banana Ball baseball barnstorming tour on July 31 and Aug. 1, and country singer Luke Combs is scheduled to perform at Albertsons Stadium on June 12, at the tail end of the budget year. Revenue sharing will increase to about $14.1 million, up from about $10 million. Colleges and universities can spend up to $21.6 million in revenue sharing, and the Boise State payments tie into “overall competitiveness” with rival programs, Dickey told board members. One unknown is the revenue Boise State will collect from the new-look Pac-12, now in its inaugural season. In time, Boise State expects to reap increased revenues from its new conference. But for this year, the university is budgeting for flat conference revenues, unchanged from its final season in the Mountain West, said Stacy Pearson, Boise State’s interim CFO. If the deficit exceeds $18 million, Boise State athletics would have to come back to the State Board for additional spending authority. The State Board approved the deficit spending plan unanimously, but not without discussion. Board member Shawn Keough — a former state senator who co-chaired the Legislature’s budget-writing Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee — said she was “really uncomfortable” with the vote. “I really don’t want to be here in a couple months or another year. Something has to give.” Board President Kurt Liebich said the deficit spending gives Boise State the flexibility it needs during a time of turmoil in college sports. The Senate has passed a college sports overhaul bill , but it is on hold in the House. “(We’re) giving you all the runway you need to figure it out, and I think you guys deserve that runway because of the sustained success you’ve had for 30 years,” said Liebich, who sits on a gubernatorial working group that has been studying the future of Idaho college athletics. Board member David Turnbull described Wednesday’s vote in stark terms. “The option is to basically put a bullet in Bronco sports if we don’t give them this runway.” The State Board is meeting at Lewis-Clark State College through Thursday.

Josh Kohl in the primary, said the three newcomers from District 25 will face a steep learning curve in writing legislation, understanding bills and working with other lawmakers in Boise. “There’s a lot of seniority-based stuff up there, so we’re going to have to work as a coalition to be effective,” Swensen said. Startin now faces Swensen in the general election. “It’s a tall order, but you just got to keep swinging at it,” Startin said of his chances on Nov. 3. Rusty Rehl/U.S. Army National Guard) Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador on Wednesday joined seven other states in announcing separate lawsuits against OpenAI, alleging the company’s chatbot ChatGPT harm. The 107-page lawsui t filed in Ada County Fourth Judicial District Court alleges that the company has harmed Idaho children and deceived adults in violation of the Idaho Consumer Protection Act . “We have watched technology giants experience tremendous growth and gains while putting consumers, especially children, at significant risk,” Labrador said in a press release. “The safety of Idaho’s children cannot be an afterthought to runaway profit or technological advancements. We will hold OpenAI accountable for their reckless priorities.” OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told the Idaho Capital Sun in an email that the company continues to improve its safeguards and respond to “misalignment.” “We’ve built industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack,” Pusateri wrote. “While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today. We’re committed to working with states on advancing pragmatic AI policies that apply to the entire AI industry — not just one company.” Attorneys general in Arkansas, Montana, Nebraska, West Virginia, Iowa, Kansas and Arizona filed similar lawsuits in their state courts Wednesday, Reuters reported. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE What’s in Idaho’s OpenAI lawsuit? Labrador, deputy attorneys general Matthew Maurer and Stephanie Guyon, and private attorneys from the Los Angeles and New York City offices of Kibler Fowler & Cave LLP brought Idaho’s lawsuit. The complaint alleges that OpenAI misled the public “into believing that OpenAI is a responsible actor and that ChatGPT was and is a safe, teen-appropriate tool that puts safety first.” “Designed to be overly agreeable and feign human compassion, ChatGPT has proven that it can be incredibly dangerous to vulnerable users, like children, and the public,” the lawsuit states. The attorneys argue the company falsely represented the safety, reliability and accuracy of ChatCPT. It also argues the company failed to disclose personal data was collected from children under 13, and failed to warn users of risk of self-harm, violence and suicide. “Given these accelerating threats, Attorney General Labrador is suing to compel OpenAI’s compliance with the Idaho Consumer Protection Act and to cease its dangerous activities that have put Idahoans in harm’s way with willfully reckless and unlawful conduct,” the press release said. The state’s attorneys are asking the court to declare OpenAI violated Idaho law, order the company to pay $5,000 to the state for each violation of the law, and pay actual damages and restitution. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior auth
items.body: The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on March 16, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) A panel of Idaho lawmakers that studied issues in the health insurance market on Wednesday formalized plans to develop legislation to address a range of issues that affect access to health care. The Idaho Health Insurers Working Group voted to tee up plans to reform prior authorization, a cost-control measure that health insurers use to deny covering certain treatments, and to target several other issues that the interim legislative committee heard about in its meetings in the last few months and through surveys it sent to insurers and health care providers. In a series of votes, the interim committee teed up a series of bills focused on health insurance that could be considered by the Legislature when it returns next January. Some of the other bills that could be drafted could address: Reducing delayed payments to providers, by setting standards for providers and insurers; Establishing uniform standards to credential health care providers through insurers; and Requiring the Idaho Department of Insurance, which regulates health insurers, to collect and present to the Legislature data about the timeliness of payments, and healthcare denial rates. That might also include information on one arbitration tool created by Congress that the state’s largest insurer, Blue Cross of Idaho, claims that a North Idaho microhospital heavily relies upon. Blue Cross argues the practice could drive up the cost of healthcare , and Congress is considering overhauling the tool. The potential prior authorization reform bill wouldn’t be the Legislature’s first attempt to address the issue, which some patients say can delay access to healthcare through drawn out timelines to issue decisions. Earlier this year, a bill, House Bill 611 , set out to require more transparency and establish timelines in the process, but it never received a committee hearing. Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, listens to proceedings during the Jan. 12, 2026, Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Prior authorization also impacts healthcare providers. Providers in Idaho reported spending more time on administrative work to respond to prior authorization requests in recent years, according to data that committee co-chairman Rep. Dustin Manwaring, R-Pocatello, summarized. In 2025, an American Medical Association survey found that 92% of physicians reported negative patient impacts caused by prior authorization processes. The committee was formed after a now-resolved contract fallout between a hospital in East Idaho, Portneuf Medical Center, and the insurer that runs the health plan for state employees, Regence BlueShield of Idaho. In the coming years, the state plans to transition Medicaid, a health insurance public assistance program for people who have disabilities or earn low-incomes, from being state-run to being managed by private health insurance companies . items.body: Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees appear inclined to keep the district’s five-day school week after discussing the matter during a board work session Tuesday. The board will vote next week to either stay on a five-day schedule or move to four-day model. The board will also consider swapping the current trimester schedule for semesters. The district began considering these and other changes in June. Four-day weeks have gained popularity across Idaho in recent years. Last school year, about two in three districts used four-day calendars. Eighteen of the state’s 76 charter schools use the model. In 2024, Nampa — similar in size to Pocatello-Chubbuck — became Idaho’s largest district to join the trend, which is most common among smaller districts. Pocatello-Chubbuck trustees favor five-day week Trustees Heather Clarke, Megan Furniss, Deanna Judy and Bill Osborn said they would vote to maintain the five-day week in Pocatello because of concerns a four-day week would negatively impact learning and be a difficult change for staff. Furniss pointed to families who rely on the district’s social services. Only a quarter of families with children who qualify for free and reduced-price lunch responded to a recent four-day week survey, she said, creating a “gaping hole” in the results. A survey of parents and district employees with 2,700 respondents found a split in community opinion: 56%, or about 1,500 respondents, said a four-day week is ideal. “In the end, public education is intended to serve every student,” not just families who can arrange childcare on Fridays, Furniss said. Osborn pointed to numbers showing that just 2% of schools nationwide are on a four-day week, convincing him that the five-day week is better. Judy called a switch “a huge jump.” She spoke about a hybrid model where students attend school two Fridays a month, but Clarke repeatedly objected, saying it wasn’t the purpose of the workshop. Meanwhile, Clarke, Furniss and Board Chair Raymond Knoff said they prefer the district’s current trimester system over semesters. Furniss cited students’ abilities to take more electives in an academic year. The board will also vote on the trimester-semester option next week. Other business Trustees also discussed a survey of more than 2,000 Pocatello-Chubbuck high school students regarding their preferred career-technical education (CTE) offerings. Culinary arts, welding and health professions were the most popular among students. Seventy-eight percent of students said it is important that their electives connect to future career pathways. Much of trustees’ discussion centered on military science, one of the least popular options on the survey. Pocatello Director of Business Jonathan Balls also presented the board with a summary of completed facilities maintenance projects, including an update on the Highland High School rebuild project. The school caught fire and saw severe damage in 2023.

items.body: The groups opposing and supporting Proposition 1, the proposed abortion rights initiative that will be on the Nov. 3 general election ballot, collected more than $2.5 million total in just under two weeks. (Photo illustration by Getty Images) The political action committee opposing Idaho’s Proposition 1 abortion rights initiative collected nearly $1.5 million since the end of September, buoyed by two large donations from churches. The Too Extreme for Idaho PAC, reported the previously announced $1 million donation from the Salt Lake City-based Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints on Oct. 8. The Roman Catholic Diocese of Boise donated another $300,000 to the PAC opposing the initiative the next day. Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions Since Sept. 29, Too Extreme for Idaho received $153,985 from 32 individual people and $1.3 million from four organizations, including the two churches. Too Extreme for Idaho has raised a total of just over $4 million, campaign finance data shows. As of Monday, the PAC supporting the initiative, Idahoans United for Women and Families, brought in more than $630,000 since Sept. 29. The largest donation came from the federal Government that Works PAC, based out of Washington, D.C, which gave $250,000. Oklahoma-based billionaire philanthropist Lynn Schusterman donated $200,000 on Sept. 30, campaign finance data shows. Since Sept. 29, the PAC received $265,290 from 81 individuals and $370,000 from three organizations. In total, Idahoans United has collected more than $5.6 million. Independent expenditures for and against Prop 1 total more than $2.5 million Groups and individuals spent more than $2.5 million combined to support and oppose Prop 1 in independent expenditures, which includes spending by organizations or individuals spent directly to support or oppose a ballot measure. The Idaho Secretary of State’s office in late September and early October began sharing a message with those filing campaign finance reports to request that any spending for or against a ballot initiative, constitutional amendment or advisory question be reported as an independent expenditure to help “voters more easily find and understand spending related to ballot measures.” The notice, first uploaded to the campaign finance reporting portal the last week of September and then updated on Oct. 7, also asked filers to amend previous campaign finance reports to classify spending related to ballot measures as independent expenditures. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) More than 80% of the wildfires that the Idaho Department of Lands has responded to this year have been caused by humans, Director Dustin Miller told an interim committee of Idaho legislators Tuesday. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE “This staggering figure just underscores the importance of not only a robust fuels mitigation program … but also a solid prevention program,” Miller told the Idaho Legislature’s Natural Resources Interim Committee during a meeting at the Idaho State Capitol in Boise. Through the end of September, a total of 10,000 acres of land that the Idaho Department of Lands is responsible for protecting has burned. (That figure does not include the larger number of acres of federal land, such as U.S. Forest Service land, that burned in wildfires this summer.) Dustin Miller is the director of the Idaho Department of Lands. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Department of Lands) The increase in human-caused fires is not new. In 2023, Miller also told a commission of statewide elected officials that he was investigating a spike in human-caused fires , the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. Miller told state legislators the costs of wildfires are high, and several legislators immediately pushed for more answers. Through the end of September, the state’s wildfire costs were a little over $47 million, of which an estimated $19.8 million could be reimbursable from other agencies the state partners with, Miller said. In addition to the financial cost to taxpayers, fires also can also threaten the safety of firefighters and the public, destroy property and burn state endowment timber lands that generate funding for public schools and other beneficiaries. There is also the cost of rehabilitation and recovery following fire and the long-term effects caused by fire. Idaho legislators ask how state can recoup costs for human-caused fires While human-caused fires aren’t new, the 80% figure grabbed the attention of several legislators. Senate Majority Leader Lori Den Hartog, R-Meridian, asked Miller if the state was doing enough to go after the people who were responsible. Natural Resources Interim Committee Co-Chair Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, asked if stronger penalties would be a deterrent. “Just something that encourages people to think a little more responsibly about how their behavior can have, not only the financial, but the environmental and property damage and all of the surrounding consequences,” Raybould said. State Rep. Britt Raybould, R-Rexburg, speaks from the floor of the Idaho House of Representatives on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Miller told the committee that the state investigates the cause of every fire and attempts to recoup funding from individuals or groups that are deemed “negligent.” Sometimes the recovery process works well, Miller said, but sometimes it can take years to recover the money, and the state doesn’t always succeed. “Oftentimes we settle for less than what the suppression costs were,” Miller said. “We really try to work with the individual and their insurance companies,” Miller added. “These are taxpayers always, and we want to recoup as much as we can back to the general taxpayer. Kalshi, an online prediction market platform, on Tuesday donated $5,000 to Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador’s campaign. The donation comes months after Labrador challenged the federal government over the state’s authority to regulate sports betting platforms. Kalshi lets users “predict” the outcome of events, including Idaho elections — and Labrador’s re-election. Read More As the 2026 Nov. 3 general election approaches, Idahoans have been asking questions about filling out ballots, write-in candidates, online voter registration searches, and more as they gear up to vote. The Idaho Capital Sun spoke to Secretary of State Phil McGrane and his staff about some of the top concerns that have arisen this election season. Here are some of the most frequently asked questions: If I don’t fill in a response to every question, does my ballot still count? Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane attends the State of the State Address at the State Capitol building in Boise on Jan. 8, 2024. (Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) Voters can skip any question or race on their ballot if they choose to. McGrane had heard concerns from voters worried that if they didn’t fill out a response to one of the ballot questions, that the rest of their ballot would be thrown out. This won’t happen, he said. “Voters are not required to vote in every race on their ballot for it to count,” the secretary of state’s office spokesperson Joe Parris said in an email. “If they skip a question or contest, the remaining selections on their ballot will still be counted.” Can I write in a candidate or write in an answer to the state gun advisory question? Prospective write-in candidates in Idaho must file a “Declaration of Intent” to run with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office, and the deadline to do so was Sept. 4. Voters may still write in a name, but that vote won’t count if it doesn’t go toward a registered write-in candidate. This year, the only write-in candidate who filed this declaration is independent gubernatorial candidate Jacob Burnett, according to the Secretary of State’s Office. For House Joint Resolution 4 , House Joint Resolution 6 , and Proposition 1 , there are only “yes” or “no” options to fill out on the ballot. The advisory question about selecting an official state gun has six choices of gun and no option to write in a response. Are signatures on absentee ballots verified, and how? Signatures on all absentee ballots are verified, Idaho Secretary of State’s Office officials said. Election staff members compare signatures on the ballots with voter registration, signature history on previous ballots, and driver’s license records to confirm a match before ballots are counted, Parris said. “Make sure you sign your own absentee ballot,” Parris said. “A common mistake is a spouse putting their return ballot in the wrong return ballot envelope.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Voters who have moved, changed their name or haven’t voted in the past four years will need to update their voter registration. items.body: All three candidates for Idaho’s top education job say that the state should be more transparent about who’s benefiting from a fledgling private school choice program. Incumbent state superintendent Debbie Critchfield, a Republican, faced challengers Becky Sundin Mitchell, a Democrat, and Teresa Roundy of the Constitution Party in a live, televised debate Monday. Idaho News 6, a Boise-based TV station, hosted the debate. The candidates agreed on many topics during the hourlong event, including whether the state should release data that shows how many recipients of the Parental Choice Tax Credit were previously enrolled in private school. They also agreed that private schools receiving taxpayer funds should be subject to similar academic reporting requirements as public schools. “It’s no different than any other government program that is funded through taxpayer dollars,” Critchfield said. “We have an expectation to know where those dollars go.” Critchfield added that the state should find out whether parents are satisfied with the education choices that they made for their children. The tax credit offers families up to $5,000 — or $7,500 if they have a disability — to offset private school tuition and other nonpublic education expenses, including homeschooling costs. Since the program launched Jan. 15, the Idaho State Tax Commission, the state agency responsible for administering the tax credit, has yet to release data that would test a key selling point of the program: that it would help students who couldn’t otherwise afford private education. “Any time that taxpayer money is used for anything, there should be accountability attached to it,” Sundin Mitchell said. “I’m concerned that we passed this tax credit system without having any accountability measures in place.” Roundy agreed. “The state should track and publicly report these figures to ensure total transparency, fiscal responsibility and equity for Idaho taxpayers,” she said. “Public funds must be used effectively and should never subsidize the wealthy at the expense of families who are genuinely struggling.” Idaho News 6 senior reporter Riley Shoemaker and neighborhood reporters Greenlee Clark and Allie Triepke moderated the debate. Candidates were given one minute to respond to each question. The candidates also discussed Idaho’s aging school funding formula, school security, facilities funding and special education, among other topics. Click here to watch the full debate. items.body: Idaho’s colleges and universities are seeking more than $170 million for capital projects — requests likely to far outstrip available funding. The money would come from the Permanent Building Fund, which receives a share of lottery dividends and collects a host of tax carveouts. The fund pays for public works projects across state government, not just on campuses. This year’s Permanent Building Fund budget came to $72.5 million. Gov. Brad Little and the Legislature cut into this budget, siphoning $48.5 million in interest earnings into a cash-strapped state general fund budget. Consequently, the state funded only $890,000 for a single capital project this year, an Idaho National Guard request. State agencies requested $229.4 million for capital requests, and most were unfunded. Nonetheless, when Idaho college and university leaders appeared before the Permanent Building Fund’s advisory council Tuesday, they took turns pitching a long list of capital projects. items.body: The Professional Standards Commission approved disciplinary actions for five Idaho educators earlier this month. The state commission oversees educator certification and investigates potential violations of Idaho’s educator ethics code. It can impose discipline on an educator’s certificate, including suspension or revocation. Here’s a closer look at the latest disciplinary actions and the educators involved. Revocations Wesley Naylor , Richfield School District Ethics violations: Not maintaining a professional relationship with students Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked In September 2025, Naylor grabbed a student’s arm and/or pushed them as they tried to walk out of the classroom after the student ignored Naylor. Naylor pleaded guilty to disturbing the peace related to the incident in December 2025. Casey Hood , Arizona Ethics violations: Failing to exemplify honesty and integrity in the course of professional practice Disciplinary action: Certificate revoked Hood surrendered her Arizona teaching certificate for five years starting in September 2025 after allegations that she modified expired individualized education plans to make it appear that required meetings had occurred when they had not. Note: Educators listed without a school district were likely not working at an Idaho school when their ethics violations occurred, though they either held or applied for an Idaho certification at some point. It’s not just a building, said Anthony Perrenoud, the program’s department chair. It’s a tool for learning. Growth in the Construction Management program was also a factor. “When we designed this building, there were 300 students” in the program, Perrenoud said. Now, it has 560 students. Inside the building The ESI Construction Management building stands out on campus for its extensive use of wood. The facility includes student workspaces, a computer lab, classrooms and conference rooms. The state controller is a constitutional officer that serves as Idaho’s chief fiscal officer and serves on the Idaho State Board of Land Commissioners, which is commonly referred to as the Land Board. The position is for a four-year term and comes with an annual salary of $128,690. Meet Democratic challenger Rakesh Mohan Mohan worked as a government auditor and evaluator for 36 years, working for state legislatures in Idaho, Washington, Louisiana and Kansas. He spent the last 21 years of his evaluation career as director of the nonpartisan Idaho Office of Performance Evaluations until he retired in June 2024 . After that, Mohan served as a visiting professor at the School of Public Policy at Boise State University. Mohan is not an accountant or IT professional, but he said his 30-plus years of experience evaluating and auditing government policy and programs has prepared him to serve as controller. He said he is running because he believes in accountability and transparency and did not want to see Woolf run unopposed, like Woolf did in the 2014 and 2018 general elections. “Since I decided to run and I started talking to people, the very first questions I get asked are, ‘Do we have a controller?
