items.body: Idaho Education News’ board of directors announced today CEO Jennifer Swindell has been named publisher and Devin Bodkin has been named COO and managing editor of the nonprofit, online news organization. Swindell founded Idaho EdNews in January of 2013 and has served as CEO and managing editor over its 14-year development. She will continue to serve as the company’s CEO. Jennifer Swindell, Idaho EdNews founder and publisher “Jennifer is an extraordinary leader and journalist,” said EdNews Board Chair Alicia Ritter. “This promotion is recognition of her success at growing an organization whose consistent and solid news reporting has elevated thoughtful and impactful discussion of education in Idaho.” Bodkin spent the last year as EdNews’ assistant managing editor, prepping for today’s promotion. Previously, he was an East Idaho reporter, blogger and editor for EdNews. He will continue to work and live in eastern Idaho. “We’re lucky to have a talent like Devin take the reins of EdNews management,” Ritter said. “His experience, talent and perspective will serve readers well as he steps into big shoes.” Swindell is an award-winning investigative journalist and editor and has been an Idaho journalist for nearly 40 years. She spent 20 years at the Idaho Statesman as a reporter, columnist and editor. She also was a director of communications for Boise State University before launching EdNews. As publisher, Swindell will set the strategic vision of Idaho EdNews and continue to be the public face of the organization. Bodkin previously was a corporate editor at the Idaho National Laboratory and a former Idaho teacher. As managing editor, he will be responsible for day-to-day operations. EdNews, a non-profit, is governed by a three-person board, including Ritter. Also serving on the board are Kim O’Connor, a former journalist and victim witness coordinator for the Ada County Prosecutor’s Office, and Stacia Albiston, a former teacher and the communications officer for the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. Devin Bodkin, Idaho EdNews COO and managing editor In other staff news, Ryan Suppe is being promoted to accountability reporter and assistant managing editor. He’ll pursue watchdog stories and assist Bodkin with day-to-day operations. Suppe was EdNews’ politics reporter. Sean Dolan will move into the politics reporter position and cover the Idaho Legislature with veteran reporter Kevin Richert, who has covered the Legislature for more than 35 years with the Idaho Statesman and Idaho Education News. Richert also will continue to write his Thursday analysis pieces and anchor the new Idaho EdNews Show, a regular podcast-video. Emma Epperly will continue to serve as EdNews North Idaho reporter, rounding out a team whose reporting reaches all corners of the state. She also follows charter school development and how policies are implemented in Idaho schools. EdNews has won multiple national and statewide awards for investigative and watchdog journalism. The website has seen record growth this past year, reaching millions of page views and social media followers. EdNews produces comprehensive and thoughtful journalism about education policy and practice in Idaho. The nonprofit is a public awareness service where parents, patrons, educators and lawmakers can find the most useful information on issues that affect Idaho’s children and their future. EdNews is committed to its mission of holding lawmakers and educators accountable for taxpayer dollars and student achievement. EdNews is free and published without advertising thanks to the generosity of the J.A. and Kathryn Albertson Family Foundation. For questions or comments, contact Jennifer at jswindell@idahoednews.org . items.body: The Boise Temple of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints as seen on Feb. 5, 2025. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun) The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints has donated $1 million to an Idaho political action committee, or PAC, opposing the abortion rights initiative on the ballot this November. The donation went to the Too Extreme for Idaho Political Action Committee, which opposes the initiative. “While The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints remains neutral toward political candidates, it actively addresses ballot initiatives it believes carry significant moral consequences,” the church said in a statement. “Accordingly, the Church has joined a coalition of like-minded organizations and individuals in Idaho to dedicate resources toward defeating Proposition 1.” Supporters and opponents of Idaho’s abortion rights initiative, Prop 1, have raised millions If passed, the voter initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion laws, enumerate rights related to reproductive health, and create liability protections for healthcare providers who provide abortion and other reproductive healthcare. The Idaho Falls radio station NewsTalk 107.9 first reported the donation on Thursday. The Idaho Capital Sun confirmed the donation with a spokesperson for the church on Friday. The large donation comes after Idaho Attorney General Raúl Labrador published an opinion in August that says churches are allowed to donate money to political campaigns — including for and against Proposition 1 — without disclosing their donors, as long as they don’t ask members to donate specifically for the campaign, Boise State Public Radio reported. Leaders from the church, widely known as the Mormon church, issued a letter against Prop 1 in September, the Salt Lake Tribune reported. The letter was read to congregations last month, the church’s assistant communications director Brian Whitlock said in an email. “Our long-held stance on abortion remains clear and unchanged,” the four-member U.S. Central Area Presidency of the LDS Church wrote in the letter. The church, which opposes elective abortions, posted its stance on abortion online . It allows for possible exemptions in cases of rape and incest, or in cases where a “competent physician determines that the life or health of the mother is in serious jeopardy,” or a “competent physician determines that the fetus has severe defects that will not allow the baby to survive beyond birth.” “Even these exceptions do not automatically justify abortion,” the statement said. “Abortion is a most serious matter. It should be considered only after the persons responsible have received confirmation through prayer.” Idaho’s abortion ban allows the procedure to prevent the death of the mother and in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report. Doctors who provide abortions outside of those exemptions face felony penalties, including minimum prison time, and potential civil lawsuits brought by family members of the aborted fetus. items.body: President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel, but on Friday, Idaho Gov. Brad Little relaxed the Gem State's inspections of the fuel during harvest. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor) Idaho Gov. Brad Little signed an executive order Friday to suspend for 30 days state inspections of dyed diesel fuel in an attempt to lower costs for farmers and ranchers, according to the governor’s office. With election pressure mounting, states move to suspend fuel taxes Dyed diesel is diesel fuel with red dye in it and is exempt from federal and state motor fuel taxes. The tax-exempt fuel is only meant for certain approved off-road uses, such as for farming equipment, construction equipment and home heating. The dye helps regulators enforce this requirement. Idaho’s average diesel price was around $6.41 per gallon as of Friday, according to AAA fuel prices. Prices for oil products have risen this year largely because of restrictions on ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz amid the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran, which have disrupted global supply chains. Diesel supplies have been in particularly short supply, NPR reported, and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries have also affected global supplies. On Monday, President Donald Trump signed an executive order to allow dyed diesel on highways and prohibit the Internal Revenue Service from imposing the typical penalties for doing so. Some state restrictions remain on the fuel. President Donald Trump hands off a newly signed executive order waiving federal taxes on red-dyed diesel to aide Natalie Harp during a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner) Little’s order signed Friday directs Idaho State Police and the Idaho Transportation Department to suspend inspection for dyed diesel while the agencies review Idaho’s policies and procedures, his office announced in a press release. The review will consider other state’s approach to dyed diesel enforcement and the agencies will make recommendations to Little for “efficient, effective, and practical inspection,” the release said. Little said in the press release that the timing of the order is meant to ease costs during harvest season. “Idaho farmers and ranchers work hard to feed our families, our country, and the world,” Little said in the release. “President Trump has made cutting red tape a priority, and Idaho is doing the same. We will continue looking for ways to give our farmers, ranchers, and working men and women on the road more freedom to do what they do best.” Legislative leaders in written statements said they supported the governor’s decision. “Idaho farmers and ranchers are facing high costs across the board, and expensive diesel is adding to the pressure during harvest,” Senate President Pro Tempore Kelly Anthon, R-Declo, said in the release. “This order provides some immediate relief while giving the state time to review these requirements and find a practical approach that supports our producers without adding unnecessary costs or red tape.” House Speaker Mike Moyle , R-Star, said suspending the inspections while the state reviews its policies “is a practical approach that puts common sense first and gives Idaho producers one less thing to worry about during harvest.” YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE. items.body: Collecting payments and convincing school districts to sign binding agreements to cover the Idaho School Benefit Trust’s $13 million shortfall has been a little bit more challenging than anticipated, Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron told EdNews on Friday. It’s been two weeks since the Fourth District Court named Cameron the rehabilitator of the trust , vesting in him full control of the trust and its assets, including the authority to liquidate assets to pay claims and liabilities. “Our focus is singular in attempting to make sure that all the claims that school district employees incurred are appropriately processed and paid for,” Cameron said. The trust, which more than 100 school districts and charter schools participated in during the 2025-26 benefit year, ran out of money this year and recorded a deficit of $10.5 million at the end of May. Blue Cross of Idaho, the trust third-party administrator for that benefit year, agreed to make an $11.9 million loan with 6% interest to pay off claims through Aug. 31. As rehabilitator of the trust, Cameron and the department have been tasked with collecting contributions from the member employers to pay off the loan, called a surplus note, to Blue Cross. Cameron was unable to share many details about what the department has learned since gaining access to the trust’s books and records on Sept. 24, but described some of the complications with corralling the more than 100 members into agreeing to either pay a lump sum or sign a 12-month binding contract agreeing to make monthly payments to cover their share of the shortfall. “Frankly, it’d have been easier for everybody if everybody paid a lump sum,” Cameron said. “But we acknowledge that for some districts that was not going to be possible, and so Blue Cross offered the monthly option in that case.” He said there have been some miscommunications and some rumors. “I think in part because maybe school districts were somewhat surprised,” Cameron said. “They shouldn’t have been, but they were.” Dean Cameron, director of the Idaho Department of Insurance, speaks to a lawmaker after an Idaho Health Insurers Working Group meeting on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho state revenues beat their forecast for the third straight month and are now more than $90 million ahead of projections to begin Fiscal Year 2027, Gov. Brad Little announced Friday. For September, general fund revenues exceeded their forecast by $39 million, or 7%, according to the September General Fund Revenue Report issued by the Idaho Division of Financial Management. Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little gives his State of the State Address from the House chambers on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s state government runs on a fiscal year calendar that begins July 1 each year. Through the first three months of Fiscal Year 2027, state revenues are now up by $90.3 million, or 6.8%. The surging revenues in this year’s state budget are a stark contrast to last year, when Little and Idaho state legislators approved near across-the-board budget cuts for almost all state agencies, programs and departments to pay for federal tax cuts President Donald Trump signed into law through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and to ensure the state passed a balanced budget, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. State revenues were also up in July and August. “Idaho’s strong revenue growth is encouraging and reflects the strength of our economy, but we must remain disciplined and make spending decisions based on what we can responsibly sustain,” Little said in a written statement Friday afternoon. “The difficult decisions we made last year put us in a stronger fiscal position, and we need to continue prioritizing the investments that matter most to Idahoans while protecting our long-term financial stability.” Income tax withholdings are driver of state revenue increase Individual income tax withholdings are a big part of the revenue increase. That law, which is still on the books , requires English to be used as “the sole language of government.” But it lists many exceptions to its requirement that government documents be in English, such as for law enforcement or for “public health and safety needs,” to ensure public schools can teach students who are learning English and to ensure colleges and so universities can “pursue educational purposes.” 2026 Voter Guide Dates to know, how-to instructions and candidate surveys for Idaho’s top contested races. Read More In this year’s general election on Nov. 3, Idaho voters will decide on whether to amend the state’s constitution to declare English as the state’s official language. But what isn’t immediately clear, some say, is whether the amendment will end existing exemptions in state law that allow languages other than English to be used by government agencies. The proposed constitutional amendment’s only exception allows the government to use other languages when required by federal law, such as in schools and, in some cases, election administration. “It’s not entirely clear, honestly, how much it would change things,” said University of Idaho law professor Richard Seamon, who has taught at the school for 30 years. The proposed amendment, passed by the Idaho Legislature to be placed on the ballot through House Joint Resolution 6 in 2025 , calls for English to be used in “all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution of the state of Idaho.” Here’s what the amendment will look like on your ballot: .indent2Container { margin-left: 1em; border-left: solid 1px var(--brand_one); padding-left: 2em; } “Shall Article X of the Constitution of the State of Idaho be amended by the addition of a new Section 8, to provide that the English language shall be the official language for the state of Idaho, and to further provide that, except as required by federal law, English shall be used in all public proceedings, public documents, public instruction, and any other public acts of any public institution in the state of Idaho?” To pass, the amendment needs support from at least 50% of voters. Idaho, a Republican supermajority-controlled state, has strong protections for gun ownership — such as not requiring permits for concealed carry in city limits. The state Legislature considered a bill this year to allow members of the public to carry concealed guns inside parts of courthouses that aren’t meant for court, like offices for county commissioners and clerks. The advisory question on the ballot this year asks voters to weigh in on the Legislature’s possible decision to declare a firearm — out of a mix of well-known Western and American guns — as Idaho’s official state gun. If Idaho declared a state gun, the recognition would grow the list of officially declared state symbols , like the state flower, the syringa; the state gem, the star garnet; or the state amphibian, the Idaho giant salamander. Ten other states have declared state guns , according to the National Rifle Association, a prominent gun lobbying group. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. items.body: U.S. Attorney for the District of Idaho Bart Davis in his Boise office. (Photo by Laura Guido/Idaho Capital Sun) Idaho’s top-ranking federal law enforcement official, U.S. Attorney Bart Davis, announced his retirement Wednesday following a long, influential legal and political career in Idaho . ‘The best job I ever had’: Bart Davis returns as Idaho’s chief federal litigator Davis, who is 71 and in his second term as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho, will retire Oct. 17, the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho said. “I am unable to overstate the privilege it has been to work with the dedicated and remarkable women and men of the U.S. Attorney’s Office,” Davis said in a written statement. “These great lawyers and support staff faithfully enforce the law, work to keep Idaho and our country safe, support our law enforcement partners and protect the civil rights of others. I am proud of the work they do every day.” President Donald Trump nominated Davis for U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho last year, and the U.S. Senate confirmed Davis on Oct. 7, 2025 – exactly one year before Davis announced his retirement. Davis previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of Idaho from 2017 to 2021 during Trump’s first term. Prior to serving as U.S. attorney, Davis practiced law in Idaho Falls and served in the Idaho Senate for 19 years. Davis, a Republican, served as Senate majority leader for 15 years, where he was regarded as a powerful and intelligent legislative leader. “Bart Davis has served the State of Idaho and our country with distinction throughout a remarkable career,” Idaho Gov. Brad Little said in a written statement. “His sound legal judgment, deep knowledge of Idaho and unwavering commitment to doing what is right have been invaluable to our state.” Davis also served as co-chairman of the 2021 Idaho Commission for Reapportionment , which was charged with redrawing Idaho’s congressional and legislative boundaries following the 2020 census to ensure political representation is proportional. During a 2025 interview with the Idaho Capital Sun, Davis called serving as U.S. attorney, “the best job I ever had.” “… to work with these people who are genuinely trying to even-handedly apply the laws of the United States of America,” Davis said. “It impressed me then, and it impresses me now.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. Brad Little gives a press conference after delivering his annual State of the State address on Jan. 6, 2025, in the Lincoln Auditorium in the Idaho Capitol. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun) The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the District of Idaho is responsible for prosecuting federal crimes in Idaho, defends the United States in civil cases and collects debts owed to the United States, the office said. In the past year under Davis’ leadership, the office said it has filed 298 criminal charges, including 103 drug trafficking cases, 89 violent crimes cases, 69 immigration cases and 22 fraud cases. “During his time as U.S. Attorney for Idaho, Bart strengthened the relationship between Idaho and the U.S. Department of Justice and represented our state with integrity and professionalism,” Little said. “ We will miss his counsel, his wisdom and his steady leadership. I am grateful for Bart’s many years of service and friendship, and I wish him all the best as he enters retirement and has more time to enjoy with his wife, children and grandchildren.” Davis and his wife, Marion, have six children and 14 grandchildren. The protest, organized by Idaho Voices for Children, took place before the governor's State of the State Address. (Photo by Christina Lords/Idaho Capital Sun) One thing we know for absolute certain in Idaho: Our people understand the value of Medicaid expansion. We voted to adopt Medicaid expansion in 2018 through ballot initiative started after years of inaction by the state Legislature, with more than 60 percent of Idaho voters supporting expanded healthcare access. When the state Legislature became very active in attempts to weaken and repeal that voter-approved expansion seemingly as soon as they could, Idahoans showed up. They traveled to Boise to let lawmakers know that the program was not a suggestion, but a mandate and more than 80,000 of our friends, family and neighbors relied on it. Idaho’s Medicaid work requirements start in January. Here’s how they will work. Some of the busiest days at the Capitol are when everyday Idahoans show up to have their voices heard on a healthcare bill when lawmakers have tried to repeal the program or institute confusing bureaucracy via work requirements. The halls are packed and hearing rooms overflow with Medicaid supporters who vastly outnumber those who advocate cuts at around 100-1 … and the one is very often not somebody from Idaho. Most Idahoans, myself included, don’t think much about the details of our health insurance until we need it. For someone with cancer, that could mean discovering at a doctor’s appointment, while scheduling a scan, or even in the middle of treatment or recovery that they no longer have Medicaid coverage due to the work requirements that will add red tape to the program starting in January. Then what? Do they delay treatment while trying to navigate the paperwork? Do they skip a follow-up appointment or prescription they can no longer afford? For most, there isn’t another insurance option waiting in the wings. These are Idahoans who already qualified for Medicaid, including people whose serious medical conditions should qualify them for a medical frailty exemption. Administrative red tape should not become another obstacle between a cancer patient and the care they need. When that happens, the consequences aren’t limited to the patient. Their families suffer too and local care providers must then care for somebody with no ability to pay the bill. It’s a terrible scenario and one Medicaid expansion has prevented from being widescale. Read More Currently, there are two ways in Idaho that marijuana, medical cannabis or other drugs can be legalized and regulated. First, the Idaho Legislature could pass a law to legalize it. Second, Idaho voters could legalize it by passing a ballot initiative. Who gets to decide is a big part of the debate over House Joint Resolution 4, or HJR 4 for short. House Joint Resolution 4 is a proposed amendment to the Idaho Constitution that would give the Idaho Legislature the sole authority and power to legalize marijuana (including medical marijuana), narcotics and other psychoactive substances. If a simple majority of voters vote “yes” for House Joint Resolution 4, Idahoans would not be allowed to bring a ballot initiative forward to legalize marijuana, medical cannabis, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. If voters vote “no” and don’t approve HJR 4, there would be no changes to the Idaho Constitution. That means Idahoans would still be able to use the ballot initiative process to legalize marijuana, narcotics or other psychoactive substances. Voters in several of Idaho’s neighboring states, including Washington, Oregon, Montana and Nevada, used ballot initiatives to legalize marijuana in those states. People have tried to do the same in Idaho. But so far, each effort has failed to meet the signature-gathering requirements to qualify for an election, the Idaho Capital Sun previously reported. He said a ballot initiative is a tool of democracy that the public has used to improve the state since the 1930s. items.body: Joleen Noble, executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank, says the nonprofit organization typically provides more than 75,000 diapers to children in need per month. (Photo courtesy of the Idaho Diaper Bank) As a mother of two small children (ages 2 and 5), there’s no need to lecture Jolleen Noble of Meridian about the cost of diapers – which could run close to $200 a month per child. And there’s no need to talk to her about other paycheck-eating costs such as daycare, medical emergencies and clothing. She knows all about the challenges of making ends meet. Noble, of course, can’t solve all of the financial problems. But as the executive director of the Idaho Diaper Bank , she’s providing some welcome relief in at least one area. And there are no forms to fill out, or financial statements to submit. “People who need diapers need our help,” she said. There are limits. Noble’s nonprofit organization will provide up to 50 diapers a month per baby, which doesn’t cover the entire cost for diapers. But it does make the monthly diaper tab less daunting. “Diapers are expensive, and they just add to the cost of everything else,” she said. The diaper bank gets a large portion of its supply from the National Diaper Bank Network, buying bulk from manufacturers and regional diaper drives. Mary Kay Link, an Idaho Diaper Bank board member for seven years, sees how the organization helps mothers and families. She volunteers with the Holy Apostles St. Vincent de Paul of Meridian , one of 43 working partners that distribute diapers. “SVDP has many single moms who work and need food and diapers to make ends meet. Saving money on diapers allows them to use the money to pay bills or put gas in their car,” she said. Noble has been the executive director for almost a year, and demands for the service are growing. “When the diaper bank started in 2014, they were giving out 8,000 diapers a month, and when I started it was 50,000 per month. Typically, we give out 75,000 to 100,000 per month … last month we gave 119,000.” Noble says that level of growth would not happen without her board of directors. “We have an incredible all-volunteer board that has helped shape Idaho Diaper Bank into what it is today,” she said. “I would not be in the position I am today, or able to do what I do, without the support, leadership and willingness to jump in wherever they are needed.” The diaper bank’s 43 partners also contribute to the success. Susan Rohrbacher sees the needed help through Parma Community Schools, which serves more than 25 babies per month. “This partnership has been especially meaningful for families of children with special needs,” she said. “The Idaho Diaper Bank is truly making a difference by easing financial stress and helping our families feel supported and cared for.” As with other nonprofit organizations, Noble sees challenges. “The biggest need is sustainable funding that allows us to grow our reach. Our funding comes from grants and in-kind donations. There is no government assistance,” she said. “Simply put, if we want to send more diapers out the door, we have to bring more diapers and funding in the door,” Noble said. “Space is becoming another challenge. As we think about serving more families and potentially expanding, sustainable funding and the capacity to store the product becomes increasingly important.” One big way individuals and businesses can help is through diaper drives. “Some of my favorite moments are seeing people in the community rally around a diaper drive,” she said. “Those drives bring in product and monetary donations, of course, but they also get people talking about diaper needs and introduce people to our mission. It’s pretty incredible to watch.” The Idaho Diaper Bank is living up to its slogan, “Changing Babies. Changing Lives.” GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE

The initiative would repeal Idaho’s abortion bans, enumerate rights related to reproductive healthcare such as access to contraceptives and IVF, and provide liability protection to doctors providing reproductive healthcare. Idaho’s existing laws ban nearly all abortions, with exceptions to prevent the death of the mother or in cases of rape and incest in the first trimester with a police report.
